architecture.tenancy_model: Deployment-level. One codebase, two Azure Web Apps, two databases, two sets of blob containers. Plus a per-hostname DB route inside server.php for a COE sub-tenant.
architecture.request_path: HTTPS -> App Service nginx (custom site config installed by startup.sh) -> PHP-FPM:9000 -> server.php (session, rate limit, CSRF scope, per-host DB routing) -> module/bootstrap.php (Composer autoload, Dotenv safeLoad, Database, csrf, password, Storage)
architecture.routing_compat: azure-nginx-default.conf reproduces the Apache .htaccess extensionless rewrite as try_files $uri $uri/ @legacy_php_route; startup.sh probes four candidate nginx config paths, copies, runs nginx -t, reloads, logs to /home/LogFiles
architecture.storage_model: blob://visibility/path references stored in the database; three visibility tiers (private/protected/public); SAS-signed URLs for browser-direct reads; authenticated streaming proxy (storage.php) for sensitive reads; permanent fallback to legacy local filesystem when a value is not a blob reference
architecture.session_state: PHP default local file handler. Cannot use the Azure Files /home mount (PHP files handler uid check fails on that CIFS mount). This is why both apps run a single worker.
security_controls: CSRF enforcement scoped to /students/, /admissions/, /cert_transs/, /staffs/, /votes/ and toggleable
per-session per-path rate limiting (20 req/10s) with allow-list

engineering_challenges.name: Restoring Apache routing semantics on nginx without touching 5,400 files
engineering_challenges.why_hard: App Service's PHP image gives no supported hook for a custom nginx site config; the config path differs between image versions and is overwritten on restart. Failure mode is a site returning 404 for every page with no obvious cause.

engineering_challenges.name: Writing an Azure Blob client by hand in legacy PHP
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Two distinct, unforgiving signing schemes (SharedKey canonical string-to-sign with strict 12-newline format and canonicalized x-ms-* headers; service SAS with its own field order and API-version pinning), both failing with an identical opaque 403. RFC-3986 path encoding must encode the path but not the separators.

engineering_challenges.name: Making an incremental migration survivable
engineering_challenges.why_hard: A straight cutover breaks every page the moment the first row updates. The design invariant - every read path falls back to the legacy local file when the value is not a blob reference - is what allowed column-by-column migration against a live database.

engineering_challenges.name: Bulk export performance against object storage
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Moving files off local disk converts fopen() into an HTTPS round trip plus TLS handshake, pushing N-file exports into the FastCGI timeout. The curl_multi scheduling loop has a subtle bug: a job failing before reaching curl consumes its slot without entering the active set, so refill must happen at the top of the iteration or a batch of failures spins with nothing in flight.

engineering_challenges.name: Multi-tenancy without a tenancy model
engineering_challenges.why_hard: The application has no tenant column. Isolation is achieved by deploying the same commit to two Web Apps with different App Settings, databases and container names, plus a per-hostname DB route for a sub-tenant. Tenant-specific behaviour therefore lives in environment variables rather than code.

decisions.name: nginx config installed by a startup script rather than a custom container
decisions.problem: App Service's built-in PHP image ignores .htaccess
decisions.reasoning: URL rewriting touches thousands of files with no test suite; a custom image means owning PHP patching for a team that wanted managed hosting
decisions.tradeoff: Coupled to App Service's internal nginx layout; could break on an image update - mitigated by probing four paths, nginx -t validation and logging
decisions.result: Extensionless routes work on both apps; startup command live in production

decisions.name: blob:// reference scheme in the database rather than storing URLs
decisions.problem: What goes in the passport column once files move to Blob
decisions.reasoning: A URL bakes account name, endpoint and container into every row, making account migration a data migration. A bare path loses the visibility tier.
decisions.tradeoff: Values are not directly usable outside the app
decisions.result: 571,040 production rows carry these references; account, endpoint and container names remain environment-configurable

decisions.name: Dual-mode storage with permanent legacy fallback
decisions.problem: Migrating hundreds of thousands of rows while serving live traffic
alternatives: a temporary shim to be removed
decisions.reasoning: PLANS.md explicitly warns not to switch uploads to Blob without supporting legacy reads
decisions.tradeoff: Permanent complexity in every read path; and it removes the pressure to finish - ebooks.fileUrl is still unmigrated
decisions.result: Safe incremental migration with residual legacy debt

decisions.name: Three containers by exposure level, prefixed per school
decisions.problem: The application mixes public brand images with private identity documents
decisions.reasoning: AGENTS.md requires treating student/staff/admission/transcript documents as sensitive by default
decisions.tradeoff: Visibility must be declared at every upload site; a wrong declaration silently over-exposes
decisions.result: Six containers live; private/protected content served via SAS or authenticated proxy

decisions.name: Hand-rolled signing rather than the Azure SDK
decisions.reasoning: The Azure PHP SDK is effectively unmaintained and would drag a dependency tree into a PHP 8.3 app with PHP-7-era assumptions
decisions.tradeoff: I own correctness and API-version pinning (REST 2021-12-02, SAS 2023-11-03); no SDK upgrade path; and this is the component most deserving of tests, which it does not have

decisions.name: Matrix deployment to both schools from one main push
decisions.tradeoff: No per-school release isolation - a bad commit reaches both universities simultaneously. fail-fast:false limits partial-failure blast radius, not bad-code blast radius.

decisions.name: Exclude the EKSU activity_log from the Azure migration
decisions.problem: After nearly seven years the EKSU audit log had grown very large; migrating it would carry its full history into paid, provisioned Azure MySQL capacity on a 25 GB server already holding 6.30 GB of live data
decisions.decision: Leave it behind; keep the historical log on the old cPanel host as a cold fallback; the Azure table starts fresh from the migration date
decisions.reasoning: Append-only log data with no transactional dependency, consulted rarely and never on a hot path - the largest thing droppable from a migration without affecting application behaviour
decisions.tradeoff: The live system no longer holds its own pre-Aug-2026 audit trail. For a system whose auditability underpinned institutional trust, answering 'what happened in 2022?' now needs an offline copy, whose retention is only as good as the old host's. BOUESTI took the opposite path and kept full history (8,471,215 rows back to 2021-05), so the two instances differ in audit depth.
decisions.result: EKSU activity_log holds 846,971 rows from 2026-08-15 onward; historical log retained off-cloud. DELIBERATE cost/scope decision, NOT data loss - an earlier draft wrongly flagged it as possible migration damage.

lessons.lesson: A bulk UPDATE on a legacy schema rewrites columns you did not name.
lessons.detail: transcript.appliedDate and transc_certificate.appliedDate are DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. The migration's UPDATE silently reset the application date on ~86,000 rows. Evidence: 37,346 transcript rows all dated 2026-08-15, of which 100% hold blob references, versus 19.4% for all other dates.
lessons.rule_adopted: Before any bulk UPDATE on a legacy schema, enumerate every ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP column and every trigger on the target tables, and either exclude those columns or pin them explicitly in the SET clause. Run data migrations against a restored copy first and diff.

lessons.lesson: Legacy compatibility is a feature until it removes the pressure to finish.
lessons.detail: The local-file fallback made a live incremental migration possible, and is exactly why ebooks.fileUrl is still 100% legacy two months later - nothing breaks, so nothing forces completion.
lessons.rule_adopted: Pair a migration fallback with an explicit completion tracker.

lessons.lesson: Object storage changes the performance model, not just the storage layer.
lessons.detail: Every fopen() becomes an HTTPS round trip. Code that was fine iterating files sequentially is not fine iterating blobs sequentially.
lessons.rule_adopted: Treat 'find every loop that touches more than a handful of files' as a mandatory planning step of any disk-to-object migration.

lessons.lesson: Platform compatibility is where lift-and-shift migrations actually fail.
lessons.detail: Not the database and not the code, but .htaccess, TLS enforcement, CAST(x AS INT), only_full_group_by, session storage on a CIFS mount, and PHP 8 throwing where PHP 7 returned false. Individually small; collectively most of the migration.

lessons.lesson: Reverts without recorded reasoning destroy decisions.
lessons.detail: Redis sessions and the staging slot were both added and removed within weeks with no recorded why. One of them is still the system's main scaling blocker.
lessons.rule_adopted: Write a two-line why in every revert commit, or an ADR.

high_confidence_quantified: Migrated two live university portals (168,000+ student records across 11.5 GB of MySQL) from cPanel/Apache to Azure App Service and Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server, now serving 22.5M+ HTTP requests and 82,000+ distinct users per month at a 0.013% 5xx rate and 100% health-probe availability.

Designed and shipped a 1,000-line Azure Blob Storage layer with hand-rolled SharedKey and SAS signing (no SDK), then migrated 675,000+ production file references across 24 columns and 11 tables on two independent production databases - 98.7% of all mapped values, with every high-volume document mapping fully migrated and no downtime.

Moved ~85.8 GB / ~1.2M user-uploaded documents off ephemeral App Service disk into access-tiered Azure Blob containers, separating private student identity documents from public assets and serving them via authenticated proxy or time-boxed signed URLs.

Migrated 87,440 transcript and certificate records across two institutions to object storage in a single day's controlled execution, using a mapping-driven, dry-run-by-default migration tool covering 14 mappings across 11 tables.

Drove adoption of a new storage abstraction across 263 call sites in 91 files of a 1.17-million-line legacy PHP codebase without an OO refactor, using procedural wrappers to preserve existing call patterns.
Built a GitHub Actions matrix pipeline deploying a single commit to two independent Azure Web Apps in parallel, replacing manual deployment for a 5,400-file PHP application.
high_confidence_non_quantified: Restored Apache .htaccess extensionless routing on nginx by authoring a custom site config and an App Service startup hook that discovers the PHP image's nginx config path at runtime, validates and reloads - avoiding both a mass URL rewrite and ownership of a custom container image.
Hardened a legacy mysqli/PDO data layer for Azure MySQL with enforced TLS, configurable port, connect timeout and CA path, auto-detecting the Azure host so local development needed no config change.
Eliminated hardcoded database and payment-gateway credentials from source control, moving all runtime secrets to Azure App Settings.

Designed an opaque blob://visibility/path reference scheme so the database stores no hostnames, endpoints or filesystem layout, and enabled a live incremental migration by making every read path fall back to the legacy filesystem.
Diagnosed from production data that a bulk migration had silently rewritten ~86,000 business timestamps via ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, establishing the root cause and exact blast radius.
requires_confirmation: Cost, performance or operational-overhead improvement versus the previous hosting - no baseline data exists.
Any specific speedup from the concurrent blob fetch - implemented, but never measured.
Reduction in manual deployment time - no before measurement.
Whether I was sole engineer on the Azure migration - Git shows me as sole author of every infrastructure file, which is strong but not conclusive.
per_institution_eksu: Migrated the EKSU student portal (135,067 student records, 6.30 GB MySQL, 153 tables) from cPanel/Apache to Azure App Service, moving 571,040 file references to Azure Blob Storage; the instance now serves 14.09M requests/month at a 0.0076% 5xx rate with 100.00% health-probe availability.

Carried the September 2026 EKSU student-union election on the migrated platform - 7,188 ballots from 5,730 voters in ~48 hours, peaking at 1,809 ballots/hour against a 962,046-request day - with no 5xx spike. (Platform and reliability are mine; the e-voting feature was built by a colleague.)
Migrated 86,116 EKSU transcript and certificate records to object storage in a single controlled execution.
per_institution_bouesti: Migrated the BOUESTI student portal (33,099 student records, 5.20 GB MySQL, 151 tables) to Azure App Service, moving 104,550 file references to Azure Blob Storage; the instance serves 8.47M requests/month at a 0.021% 5xx rate with 99.99% health-probe availability.
Implemented per-hostname database routing for BOUESTI's third tenant (portalcoe/ptpportal to a separate COE database), the more complex of the two multi-tenant cases.

Verified migration completeness directly against the BOUESTI production database: 100% of rows touched on migration day were blob-backed against 0% of all others - the cleanest available proof that the migration executed as designed.
two_delivery_framing: Delivered an Azure migration and object-storage rollout to two universities from a single codebase and a single CI matrix - separate databases, container sets and App Service plans - covering 168,166 student records and 82,176 distinct monthly users, at 98.70% file-migration completeness across both estates.

presentation_guidance.credibility_risk: Headline figures are large enough that a recruiter may assume they are invented, especially alongside a two-person team. Manage deliberately.
presentation_guidance.currency_figure_hazard: The NGN 65.51bn payment figure is PROCESSED volume, not revenue generated or captured. Naira is hard for UK readers to size, and it invites 'if your system handles that, why are you applying here?'
rules: Lead with transaction and user counts, not currency: '1.79M payment transactions', '82,000 monthly users'
If using currency, convert to GBP at a stated rate and date, and always use the verb 'processed' - never 'generated' or 'earned'
State the two-engineer team size as an asset: scale and team size explain each other
Put verifiable technical figures first: 675,590 migrated references, 263 call sites, 22.5M requests, 0.013% 5xx
Keep this JSON and section 23 to hand - every number has a stated source, window and calculation, which converts a credibility problem into an advantage

junior_labelling_guidance.verdict: Reasonable to label pre-2020 undergraduate and startup work as junior-level. Accurate, fills timeline, shows progression.
junior_labelling_guidance.caution: Do NOT let 'junior' bleed into this project - six years of production ownership, two institutions, 22.5M requests/month. Date it from 2020 and title it founding engineer / co-founder / lead engineer.
junior_labelling_guidance.premise_check: The perception that a 'junior developer' title helps in the UK is more likely about recognisable employment STRUCTURE than the word 'junior'. Screeners look for a checkable employer, a defined role and date ranges. Make this project read as structured employment (registered company, named role, clear dates, two named institutional clients).
junior_labelling_guidance.do_not: Do not omit the earlier period - gaps invite more questions than modest early roles.

interview_stories.situation: Auditing production data two months after a storage migration I had run.
interview_stories.task: Establish real usage volumes for transcript and certificate requests.
interview_stories.action: Yearly breakdown showed 41,835 transcript requests in 2026 vs ~1,500-5,000 in prior years - implausible. Monthly put 39,035 in August; daily put 37,346 on 15 August, the exact date of my migration. information_schema showed appliedDate declared ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. Correlation: of the 37,346 rows stamped that day, 100% held blob references, vs 2,926 of 15,111 for every other date.
interview_stories.result: Confirmed my migration had silently rewritten the application date on ~86,000 records. Reported it rather than quietly correcting the statistic.
interview_stories.evidence: schema definition, correlation query, commit date

interview_stories.theme: Architecture / making an irreversible change reversible
interview_stories.situation: 571,000+ rows referencing files on disk, on a live system with no tests.
interview_stories.action: Chose an opaque blob:// reference plus the invariant that every read path falls back to the legacy file - preview, download, ZIP, PDF, delete - enabling table-by-table migration with a dry-run-by-default tool.
interview_stories.result: 571,040 references migrated, zero legacy remaining, no downtime.
interview_stories.reflection: The fallback also removed pressure to finish; ebooks is still unmigrated. Pair it with a completion tracker.

interview_stories.theme: Platform constraints / knowing when not to rewrite
interview_stories.situation: After lift-and-shift every internal link 404'd because nginx ignores .htaccess.
interview_stories.action: Rejected rewriting URLs across 5,427 untested files and rejected a custom container image; built an nginx config installed by a startup script probing four candidate paths with nginx -t validation and durable logging.
interview_stories.tradeoff: Coupled to App Service's internal layout; could break on an image update - which is why it validates and logs.

interview_stories.theme: Performance / understanding a changed cost model
interview_stories.situation: Pages ZIPping several hundred student documents started timing out after the storage cutover.
interview_stories.action: Diagnosed each fopen() had become an HTTPS round trip plus TLS handshake; built materializeMany() on curl_multi with a bounded in-flight window, streaming to disk with per-item failure isolation. The non-obvious part was slot refill at the top of the iteration.

interview_stories.content: Why I hand-rolled Azure SharedKey and SAS signing rather than using the SDK: the PHP SDK is effectively unmaintained and would pull a dependency tree into a PHP 8.3 app with PHP-7-era assumptions. Cost: I own correctness of two unforgiving signing schemes with pinned API versions and no test coverage - the piece I would write tests for first.

The September 2026 student-union election ran on this platform: 7,188 ballots from 5,730 voters over ~48 hours, peaking at 1,809 ballots/hour, against 962,046 requests on the busiest day. Response time rose to ~2s and 5xx did not spike.
interview_stories.honesty_note: I built the platform; a colleague built the voting feature. 100% health-probe availability came with no HA and a single worker, so the margin was thinner than the numbers suggest.

interview_stories.theme: A decision I can no longer defend
interview_stories.content: I added Redis-backed sessions and removed them the next day; added a staging slot and removed it eight weeks later. Neither commit message records why. The session decision still constrains the system. The lesson is cheap and concrete: a two-line why in a revert commit, or an ADR.

interview_stories.situation: One codebase had to serve two universities with completely separate data, documents and users.
interview_stories.task: Isolate them without a tenant column, which the application has never had.
interview_stories.action: Isolation at deployment time rather than in code: the same commit deploys to two App Service instances via a CI matrix, each with its own database, its own three blob containers and its own App Settings. BOUESTI additionally carries a third tenant through per-hostname routing in server.php to a separate coeikere-db.
interview_stories.result: Both run in production off one commit stream - 14.09M and 8.47M requests in 31 days, with the storage migration executing independently against each (571,040 and 104,550 references).
interview_stories.tradeoff: Tenant-specific behaviour lives in environment variables rather than code, invisible to anyone reading the repository, and a bad commit reaches both universities simultaneously. Right call for two tenants, wrong one for ten.

interview_stories.situation: Needed to show the blob migration had actually completed, not just that the script exited cleanly.
interview_stories.action: Queried both production databases for the ratio of blob:// values to surviving legacy paths, per column.
interview_stories.result: Every high-volume document mapping fully migrated on both instances; 98.70% of all mapped values overall. BOUESTI gave the cleaner proof of when it ran - 1,324 rows stamped 2026-08-15, 100% blob-backed, versus 0% of all other rows.
interview_stories.why_good: Shows verification against production rather than trust in a script, and it is the same query that surfaced the timestamp defect in S1.

portfolio_material.overview: A legacy PHP/MySQL academic portal serving two Nigerian universities - ~135,000 student records, 1.9M payment transactions, 5.5M result rows - moved from shared cPanel hosting onto Azure, with ~85 GB of sensitive student documents moved from application disk into object storage, while the system stayed live through an admissions cycle, a fee cycle and a student-union election.
portfolio_material.challenge: ~1.17M lines of procedural PHP across 5,427 files, 5,039 raw mysqli_query() call sites, no test suite, assuming Apache rewriting, local filesystem writes and MariaDB dialect tolerance. It could not go down, and it could not be rewritten.
portfolio_material.my_role: Cloud migration and storage platform engineer - not the application's author (121 of 155 commits belong to a colleague).

Storage: dependency-free Blob client, three-tier visibility, opaque blob:// references, authenticated proxy, concurrent materialisation, permanent local fallback
Delivery: GitHub Actions matrix, secrets in App Settings
what_i_would_improve_next: Shared session store (Redis or DB handler) - the single blocker to horizontal scaling
Managed Identity + RBAC to retire the long-lived storage account key
A test suite for the signing code
Finish the ebooks migration and add a completion tracker
Enable MySQL HA and a second App Service worker
Rewrite repository history to shed the 261 GB .git

audit_method_notes.database_access: mysql client with --init-command="SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY" against eksu-db (2026-10-13) and bouesti-db (2026-10-14). Only SELECT, COUNT, SUM, GROUP BY and information_schema reads. No write, DDL, migration or administrative statement was executed. BOUESTI credentials were read from bouesti-app-prod App Service settings at the user's instruction and resolve to the same server-administrator account on the same Flexible Server.
audit_method_notes.azure_access: az CLI read-only: webapp show, appsettings list restricted to names, mysql flexible-server show, storage account list, monitor metrics list.
audit_method_notes.recovered_document: MODERNIZATION_PROGRESS.md (470 lines) deleted from the working tree 2026-08-20, recovered via git show 5c4f5274^:MODERNIZATION_PROGRESS.md. Session entries signed 'Claude' indicate AI-assisted sessions; commit authorship was used to attribute the work they describe.
audit_method_notes.diffstat_caveat: My 33 commits show ~40,596 insertions / ~38,947 deletions across 1,409 file-paths, inflated by commit 62b5805f vendoring Predis and 3008db2a reverting it, plus cbf3b356 removing 85 committed upload files. File-level ownership is the reliable evidence, not line counts.
metric_caveats: information_schema.table_rows is an InnoDB estimate, used only for the size overview; headline counts use exact COUNT(*)
paymentAmount is varchar and non-Successful rows contain non-amount values; payment totals restricted to paymentStatus='Successful'
transcript/transc_certificate appliedDate values dated 2026-08-15 are migration artefacts, not application dates
'distinct users' counts distinct activityUser identifiers with at least one logged event
audit_method_notes.pii_handling: Student and staff identifiers, email addresses and user-agent strings were encountered during schema inspection and are deliberately excluded from all outputs. Every figure is an aggregate.
audit_method_notes.correction_log: The 2026-10-13 draft stated 'zero legacy paths remaining in the migrated columns'. That overstated completeness: the legacy side of leave_of_absence.attachedFile had not been queried, and it holds 5,906 legacy values on EKSU and 352 on BOUESTI. Completeness is now reported as 98.70% with the four unmigrated mappings itemised; claim C4 and the corresponding CV bullet were restated. No other figure changed.

caveats: DO NOT sum table counts: EKSU's 153 and BOUESTI's 151 are the same schema deployed twice, not 304 distinct tables. The same applies to any codebase measure (5,427 PHP files, 263 call sites) - built once, deployed twice, never doubled.

Combined distinct user (82,176) and payer (285,421) counts are the weakest sums: adding two distinct-counts is only exact if the populations are disjoint. Identifier formats make overlap very unlikely but it was not cross-matched (would mean handling personal data for no analytical gain). Treat as upper bounds.
Payment totals are full historical figures predating the Azure migration and this contribution.
Blob storage totals (~1,197,452 blobs / ~85.77 GB) are account-wide measurements, NOT sums - they cannot be split per school.

context_only_claims.claim: EKSU has been publicly ranked among Nigeria's leading state universities during the period this system has served it: 3rd best state university (Webometrics 2021), later cited as 2nd best state university, and in 2025 described by the Ekiti State Government as the leading state university, citing 12th of 270 Nigerian universities.
context_only_claims.causal_link_evidence_level: UNVERIFIED - rests on verbal remarks reported by institutional staff, with no document, citation or assessor finding. Rankings are multi-factor and no methodology isolates a student portal's contribution.
context_only_claims.safe_wording: Built and operated the student records and payments platform for Ekiti State University from 2019 - a period during which the institution was ranked among Nigeria's leading state universities.
context_only_claims.never_write: Any phrasing stating or implying the system caused or materially contributed to the ranking. It is unfalsifiable, and it would make a reader retrospectively doubt the verifiable evidence (675,590 migrated references, 22.5M monthly requests). Trading the most verifiable evidence for the least.
context_only_claims.interview_only: If asked, may add that institutional staff credited the portal as a contributing factor - spoken, attributed, framed as THEIR assessment, not the candidate's claim.
